name: Mughal imperial army (1526-1739)

weightNotes.aggression: Expansion was continuous from Babur to Aurangzeb (Panipat 1526, Chittor 1567-68, the Deccan campaigns 1681-1707), but Gommans (Mughal Warfare) stresses that much of it was won by negotiation, co-option and siege rather than battle. Moderately high.
weightNotes.maneuver: The army moved as a vast camp-city: at Karnal (1739) a war camp of about 300,000 including non-combatants, 3,000 guns and 2,000 elephants, which spent a month encamped outside Delhi before moving (Karnal page). Slow; Babur's small 1526 army was the exception.
weightNotes.flanking: Turko-Mongol tulughma flank attacks: at Panipat (1526) 'musket and cannon pinned Ibrahim's centre while horse archers harried the flanks and rear' (Panipat page).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Siege was the main form of war (Gommans): Chittor took four months with 5,000 builders digging sabats and mines (Chittorgarh page); in the Deccan, Ramsej alone took seven years (Deccan wars page). High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The Timurid battle order of vanguard, centre, wings and reserve was kept, with the emperor or prince in the centre (Gommans). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: A news-writer network existed, but field intelligence and reaction were slow: after Nadir Shah crossed the Khyber 'it was two months before any decisive action was taken' (Karnal page). Middling-low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Low by evidence: Mughal armies broke when the commander vanished, before heavy losses. Samugarh 1658: after Rustam fell and Dara dismounted from his elephant, his 50,000-60,000 fled (Samugarh page); Karnal 1739: the imperial army was defeated within three hours (Karnal page). Contingents followed their mansabdar and habitually fell short of paper strength (Mansabdar page; Gommans). No battle gives a loss share at the break; 0.1 is a judgment. Rajput contingents fought to the death (Samugarh) but were a minority.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Mounted archers, matchlock infantry, an artillery park under its own commander outside the mansabdari system, war elephants and river fleets (Mughal Army page). Arms were assembled rather than integrated, so 0.6.
weightNotes.initiative: Mansabdars led their own contingents and princes ran whole campaigns, but loyalty was conditional and coordination poor (Gommans; Mansabdar page). Moderate-low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: The camp-city carried its own markets and was fed by banjara grain carriers (Gommans), letting it sustain sieges for years; the cost was slowness, and the Deccan war of 1681-1707 ran far beyond what revenue could support. Moderately high.

summary: An imperial army raised mainly through mansabdars, officers ranked by the number of horsemen they had to maintain and paid by revenue assignments (jagirs), with Turkic, Afghan, Persian and Rajput heavy horse archers at its core, a separately commanded artillery park, matchlock infantry, elephants and river fleets. Babur's founding victories combined a laager of chained carts and guns in the centre with flanking horse archers. Under Akbar and his successors war meant slow advances by a huge moving camp, sieges of hill forts and negotiated submissions, with battle as a last resort.
whyItWorked: Against Indian armies built around elephants and cavalry without gunpowder, the cart laager with guns and flanking horse archers was decisive (Panipat 1526: Ibrahim and 20,000 of his men killed; Khanwa 1527). Scale, money and siegecraft then let the empire reduce fortress after fortress (Chittor 1568) and co-opt defeated elites as mansabdars.
whereItFailed: Against mobile enemies who refused battle: the Marathas' roving bands outlasted Aurangzeb's 26-year Deccan war of sieges, and the Ahoms beat a Mughal river fleet at Saraighat (1671). Against a professional gunpowder army it collapsed: Nadir Shah destroyed the army at Karnal (1739) in three hours and sacked Delhi. Contingent loyalty made succession wars (Samugarh 1658) decide by defection.

sources.title: Gommans, Mughal Warfare: Indian Frontiers and High Roads to Empire 1500-1700 (Routledge, 2002)
